How the Eukaryotyping distance ensemble works

Angel Luís Robles Fernández

Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology and Center for Ecological Research, University of Kansas
Source: vignettes/algorithm.Rmd
algorithm.Rmd

This vignette explains the three distance methods that make up the Eukaryotyping ensemble. The methods were first published by Barratt et al. (2019) (doi:10.1017/S0031182019000581) for genotyping Cyclospora cayetanensis from MLST data, and are reimplemented here in C++17 with RcppParallel.

Notation

Let:

  • \(n\) be the number of isolates (samples)
  • \(L\) be the number of loci
  • For locus \(j\), \(\mathcal{A}_j\) is the set of observed alleles across all samples
  • For isolate \(i\) and locus \(j\), \(\mathbf{g}_{ij}\) is the multiset of alleles carried by that isolate (size up to \(\text{MOI}_j\), the maximum multiplicity for that locus)
  • \(p_{ja}\) is the empirical frequency of allele \(a\) at locus \(j\)
  • \(H_{\nu j}\) is the entropy of locus \(j\)

1. Heuristic distance (euk_heuristic_distance)

The heuristic distance is Barratt’s unsupervised mixture-model distance. For each pair of isolates \((i, k)\) and each locus \(j\), a per-locus delta \(\delta_{ik}^{(j)}\) is computed; the overall distance is the sum of per-locus deltas.

Per-locus delta

Let \(S_{ij}\) be the set of distinct alleles carried by isolate \(i\) at locus \(j\). Define:

  • \(x = |S_{ij}| + |S_{kj}|\) — total distinct allele count
  • \(y = |S_{ij} \cap S_{kj}|\) — number of shared distinct alleles
  • \(n = \min(|S_{ij}|, |S_{kj}|)\)
  • \(m_j\) — a per-locus tuning parameter (default 1)

A frequency-informed penalty \(P\) moderates the contribution of shared alleles that are rare:

\[ P = \begin{cases} \Bigl(\frac{\#\{r : S_{ij} \cap S_{kj} \subseteq S_{rj}\}}{n_{\text{nonmissing},j}}\Bigr)^2 & y > 0 \\[4pt] 1 & y = 0 \end{cases} \]

where \(n_{\text{nonmissing},j}\) is the number of isolates with at least one non-missing allele at locus \(j\).

The per-locus delta for diploid loci (\(\text{ploidy} > 1\)) is:

\[ \delta = H_{\nu j} \cdot \Bigl( \delta_{\text{raw}} \cdot \mathbb{I}(\delta_{\text{raw}} > 0) + P \cdot \mathbb{I}(\delta_{\text{raw}} = 0) \Bigr) \cdot k \]

where \(k = 1\) if \(y = 0\) and \(k = P\) otherwise, and \(\delta_{\text{raw}}\) is a piecewise integer function of \(x\), \(y\), \(n\), and \(m_j\) that implements the original Barratt lookup table (see src/eukaryotyping.cpp:sub_per_locus() for the exact mapping).

For haploid loci the expression simplifies to:

\[ \delta = H_{\nu j} \cdot 2x \cdot \mathbb{I}(y = 0) \cdot k \]

with the same \(k\) convention. The entropy \(H_{\nu j}\) is the Shannon entropy of the empirical allele distribution:

\[ H_{\nu j} = -\sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_j} p_{ja} \log_2 p_{ja} \]

Missing-locus imputation

A pair of isolates that share no comparable locus (both missing) cannot contribute to the sum. Barratt’s two-pass mean procedure fills these entries:

  1. For each isolate with a missing locus, find all complete isolates whose allele sets match at every non-missing locus. Impute the missing-locus delta as the mean of those matched isolates’ deltas.
  2. If no match exists, impute using the global mean of the locus.
  3. A second pass catches any rows that remain partially empty after the first pass, re-imputing against the first-pass results.

The final distance for pair \((i, k)\) is:

\[ D_{ik}^{(H)} = \sum_{j=1}^{L} \delta_{ik}^{(j)} \]

2. Bayesian distance (euk_bayesian_distance)

Plucinski’s naive-Bayes distance evaluates, for each pair \((i, k)\), three log-likelihoods per locus corresponding to three relatedness hypotheses.

Per-locus log-likelihoods

Let \(\mathbf{v}_{ij}\) be the allele values (not the set, but the actual observed alleles, with multiplicities) carried by isolate \(i\) at locus \(j\), and let \(p_{ja}\) be the empirical frequency of allele \(a\) as above.

Hypothesis 0 — unrelated:

Both isolates draw all their alleles independently from the locus allele frequencies:

\[ \ell_0 = \sum_{a \in \mathbf{v}_{ij}} \log p_{ja} + \sum_{a \in \mathbf{v}_{kj}} \log p_{ja} \]

Hypothesis 1 — share one allele:

The pair shares exactly one allele; the shared allele is the most likely one. For every pair of positions \((u, v)\) where \(v_{iju} = v_{kjv}\), compute:

\[ \ell_{1,uv} = \ell_0 - \log p_{j,v_{iju}} \]

and take \(\ell_1 = \max_{uv} \ell_{1,uv}\). If no shared allele exists, \(\ell_1 = \log(\epsilon \cdot \min(p_{\text{obs}}))\), where \(\epsilon\) is the estimated allele-capture failure rate (default 0.3072, estimated by Joel Barratt in May 2019) and \(\min(p_{\text{obs}})\) is the smallest frequency among the alleles carried by the pair.

Hypothesis 2 — share both alleles (diploid loci only):

Both isolates share a pair of alleles (multiset equality). For every pair of 2-subsets \((\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})\) of \(\mathbf{v}_{ij}\) and \(\mathbf{v}_{kj}\) that are equal as multisets:

\[ \ell_{2,\mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}} = \bigl(\ell_0 - \log p_{j,a_1} - \log p_{j,a_2}\bigr) + \sum_{a \in \mathbf{v}_{kj}} \log p_{ja} \]

and \(\ell_2 = \max \ell_{2,\mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}}\). If no multiset equality exists:

\[ \ell_2 = \log\bigl[(\epsilon \cdot \min(p_{\text{obs}}))^{2 - n_{\text{shared}}}\bigr] \]

where \(n_{\text{shared}}\) is the number of distinct allele values shared by the two subsets.

Posterior and distance

The per-locus log-likelihoods are summed across loci:

\[ s_0 = \sum_{j} \ell_0^{(j)}, \quad s_1 = \sum_{j} \ell_1^{(j)}, \quad s_2 = \sum_{j} \ell_2^{(j)} \]

These are normalised to a posterior over the three hypotheses:

\[ \Pr(h \mid \text{data}) = \frac{e^{s_h}}{e^{s_0} + e^{s_1} + e^{s_2}}, \quad h \in \{0, 1, 2\} \]

The distance is the posterior expected number of shared-allele hypotheses:

\[ D_{ik}^{(B)} = 0 \cdot \Pr(0) + 1 \cdot \Pr(1) + 2 \cdot \Pr(2) \in [0, 2] \]

Values near 0 indicate the pair appears unrelated; values near 2 suggest complete allelic sharing.

3. Ensemble distance (euk_ensemble_distance)

The heuristic and Bayesian distances operate on different scales and have different sensitivities. The ensemble combines them via fractional rank averaging, a copula-style summary that is invariant to monotone transformations of either distance.

For an \(n \times n\) distance matrix \(D\), let \(U\) be the set of \(\binom{n}{2}\) unordered upper-triangular entries. Assign fractional ranks:

\[ r(D)_{ik} = \frac{\text{rank of } D_{ik} \text{ among } U} {|U| + 1} \]

so that \(r(D)_{ik} \in (0, 1)\). The ensemble entry is:

\[ D_{ik}^{(E)} = \frac{r\bigl(D^{(H)}\bigr)_{ik} + r\bigl(D^{(B)}\bigr)_{ik}}{2} \]

Values near 0 indicate both methods agree on high similarity; values near 1 indicate strong divergence.

References

Barratt JLN, Plucinski M, Nascimento F, et al. (2019) “A Genotyping Approach to Determine the Geographic Origin and Relatedness of Cyclospora cayetanensis” Parasitology, doi:10.1017/S0031182019000581.
